summary: Deep technical triage of KV layer saturation and backpressure during long-context sessions. Identified likely causes: prefix collision hotspots, TTL/eviction policy misalignment with workload, and paging under memory pressure. Proposed repro steps, telemetry captures, and short-term mitigations including prefetching and fenwick-like prefix sharding; longer-term options discussed: Dedicated capacity, quantization tradeoffs, and on-prem memory tuning.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-30 14:00 UTC
Duration: 72 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Daniel Kim (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (HelixMed - ML Platform), Markus Engel (HelixMed - SRE), Lydia Chen (HelixMed - CTO)
---
Summary (auto):
Redwood and HelixMed walked through a consistent repro where long chat sessions with repeated prefixes cause KV spillover, large paging events, and increased tail latency. Discussed TTL/eviction tuning, prefix sharding, and a short-term canary to disable certain heuristics. Agreed on telemetry captures and tests.
---
[00:00] Sofia (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros then Dan will jump into the runtime traces you shared.
[00:18] Priya (HelixMed): Hi, thanks. We'll start, we sent three traces and a link to the zenbench sheet, right? I think it's in the invite.
[00:25] Daniel (Redwood SE): Yeah I pulled the link, got the traces — thanks. I skimmed the pprof output; there's a clear spike around the 1200s mark corresponding to a burst of long-context generation.
[00:40] Markus (HelixMed): Right that's our conversational summarization pipeline, the convo context grows to ~50k tokens in some cases, and we see latencies jump and then occasional 503s.
[00:52] Lydia (HelixMed): We mainly want to understand: is this a KV eviction issue, or is there something at the runtime/batching layer causing backpressure?
[01:05] Daniel: Good question. From the stack traces it looks like a combination. The KV layer reported repeated evictions + a paging thread kicking in. There's also sustained kernel sleeps while waiting on IO, so spill to disk seems likely.
[01:20] Sofia: Quick note — Helix is on our Dedicated beta with VPC peering, right? Which flavor of Redwood runtime are they running?
[01:28] Priya: We're on the dedicated pool in us-east-1, 8xA100 equivalent, private VPC with our own NAT. Using the default eviction TTL and default prefetch heuristics.
[01:38] Daniel: Ok that helps. Default heuristics assume prefix reuse is moderate; your workload looks prefix-heavy — many sessions reuse a handful of long prefixes and then append long user content. That pattern can cause hotspots where multiple prefixes push the same KV buckets.
[01:53] Markus: Hotspots meaning collisions? Like different conversations mapping to same slot?
[01:57] Daniel: Exactly. We shard prefixes into buckets and keep a per-bucket LRU. If many heavy prefixes land in the same shard, eviction churn increases and active KV pages can be thrown out, then re-prefetched, which causes paging churn and latency spikes.
[02:15] Priya: Hmm our prefixes are often system messages with consistent phrasing across customers, so yeah reuse is high.
[02:22] [02:22] Speaker 3: there's also an observation of higher CPU syscall time during the spill windows - not purely GPU bound.
[02:30] Daniel: Right, memory pressure moves us into spill/paging which is dominated by host IO. We also saw some kernel-level thrashing in the trace where background GC and page reclaim increase latencies.
[02:45] Lydia: Could quantization cause this? We're using int8 quantized models for infer.
[02:50] Daniel: Quantization affects memory footprint per KV item slightly — int8 helps reduce memory for model weights, but the KV cache still stores key/value entries (float kv vectors), so quantization of weights alone doesn't remove KV memory pressure. However, using model variants with smaller KV sizes or enabling KV compression can help. We have a compact-kv feature in preview — but it's not enabled on your pool.
[03:10] Priya: We noticed that enabling aggressive batch sizes helped throughput but aggravated tail latency. Any advice?
[03:17] Daniel: That's classic trade-off: larger batches increase GPU utilization but increase queueing latency when backpressure happens. Continuous batching attempts to balance it, but under KV thrash continuous batching can worsen tail latency because pending requests wait for batch completion while the KV misses cause per-request serialization.
[03:35] Markus: So immediate mitigations?
[03:37] Daniel: Short-term: reduce max batch size for your heavy long-context routes, increase KV TTL for known-hot prefixes, and enable prefix sharding adjustments to spread reuse across more buckets. Also enable our prefetch heuristic for long prefixes — it will fetch anticipated KV entries earlier.
[03:55] Sofia: We'll put these in proposed changes. For Dedicated customers we can also recommend bumping KV memory allocation in the node config.
[04:04] Priya: I can try TTL + batch size changes. For the prefix sharding, is that a config we can toggle?
[04:10] Daniel: Yes it's a runtime flag in the service config: kv.prefix_shard_count and kv.prefetch_window. Increasing shard_count from default 256 to 1024 in your pool could reduce collisions. But that increases metadata and may slightly increase CPU overhead.
[04:24] [04:24] Speaker 2: (mumble) we also saw hot GC cycles in the host, the tenancy is shared?
[04:30] Daniel: You're on dedicated GPU but host-level processes still run. If you want full isolation, Private on-prem or our Private VPC with dedicated hosts avoids noisy neighbor effects more.
[04:42] Lydia: That ties to networking — our monitoring shows occasional reconnects between the VPC peered subnet and the infra. Could that exacerbate paging/backpressure?
[04:50] Daniel: Network blips cause retransmits for KV fetches and can amplify backpressure because requests stall waiting for a KV page. For on-prem deployments we recommend colocating KV store with compute or enabling local disk cache to reduce cross-host fetches.
[05:05] Priya: Any risks to changing shard count live?
[05:09] Daniel: It's safe to change but it requires a rolling update to the runtime; during the update you may see transient cache warms. We'll guide you through a canary: change in a small subset of nodes, monitor tail latency and evictions, then roll.
[05:22] Markus: The traces show a periodic pattern: latency spikes every ~6 minutes when a scheduled analytics job kicks off. Could that be garbage collection in the model runtime?
[05:30] Daniel: Could be; also consider bursty prefix reuse patterns where that analytics job opens many sessions with similar system prompts. If a non-user job writes data into the same prefix namespace it can evict user prefixes. We recommend namespace separation and prefix namespacing per tenant/job.
[05:47] Priya: We're using a shared prefix naming scheme — ok we'll change that and see.
[05:51] [05:51] Sofia: Quick interjection — on the quantization front, one medium-term option is mixed-KV precision so hot KV entries stay higher precision, cold entries compressed. That reduces memory pressure without degrading quality significantly. It's in roadmap; we can discuss pilot.
[06:10] Lydia: Sounds good. You mentioned telemetry captures earlier — what exactly do you need to reproduce?
[06:15] Daniel: We need pprof heap/proc profiles, runtime evictions log, the KV eviction counters, and a sampling of request payloads (scrubbed). Also a short benchmark harness that recreates the long chat growth so we can run on our side. If you can also capture 'kv.prefetch_hits' metric over time that's helpful.
[06:35] Priya: We can share the traces and anonymized prompts. Concern on sharing raw traces — any guidance?
[06:40] Sofia: We'll sign an NDA addendum if needed; but anonymized is fine. Use the shared s3 link in the invite.
[06:49] Daniel: For repro steps, I'd like you to run two workloads: 1) long single-session growth to 50k tokens and 2) many short sessions that reuse the same system prompt in parallel. That helps us isolate prefix hotspot vs long-context pressure.
[07:05] Markus: Recommended monitoring thresholds to catch early?
[07:08] Daniel: Watch 'kv.evictions/sec', 'kv.page_in_latency_p50/p95', 'host.io_wait', and 'runtime.batch_queue_depth'. Set alerts on kv.evictions/sec > 50 and page_in_p95 > 200ms.
[07:22] [07:22] Speaker 1: minor audio drop — sorry.
[07:27] Priya: On the note of paging, are there disk formats you'd recommend? We're on EBS gp3 volumes.
[07:33] Daniel: For heavy paging workloads we suggest NVMe local ephemeral where possible; EBS gp3 can work but you'll see amplification. Also size the ephemeral cache partition to fit your typical working set with headroom.
[07:46] Lydia: Is there any software knob to avoid complete spill to disk? Maybe partial eviction algorithms?
[07:52] Daniel: We have a 'soft-evict' that marks entries as candidates and allows quick rehydrate from a compressed in-memory slab — effectively a two-tiered memory. That reduces IO on rehydrate but increases memory overhead. It's configurable per-route.
[08:07] Priya: Can we try smaller batch + soft-evict + increased shard count as a triage?
[08:12] Daniel: Yes, that's a reasonable short-term mitigation. We'll provide a cookbook with the exact runtime flags.
[08:17] Sofia: I'll add cookbook to next steps.
[08:20] [08:20] Customer question: any impact on model quality if we use aggressive KV compression?
[08:26] Daniel: Slight risk for edge cases where KV precision maps to subtle token choice, but in most summary/assistant tasks we see negligible quality differences. We recommend A/B tests on your prompt set. Redwood Optimize can run a quick eval suite.
[08:40] Priya: On the A/B, how long to detect regressions? We need to avoid hallucination regressions.
[08:45] Daniel: For safety target a two-week rolling eval on a seeded prompt corpus; if you have guarded prompts (gold set) you can detect quality drift quickly.
[08:55] Markus: There's also an operational question: if we move to Private on-prem, does the KV eviction behaviour change?
[09:00] Daniel: Behaviorally no, same runtime, but on-prem you control memory sizing, local NVMe, and network topology, so you can eliminate remote KV fetch latency and adjust memory so eviction rarely occurs.
[09:12] Lydia: Ok makes sense.
[09:15] [09:15] Daniel: A couple of interesting anomalies I noticed: in your traces the eviction counters spike immediately after a burst, but the re-add rate is also high — that means items are being evicted and re-fetched repeatedly. We suspect two causes: prefix collision hotspots and prefetch_window being too small so we miss the right entries.
[09:33] Priya: How would prefetch window cause this?
[09:36] Daniel: If the prefetch only looks ahead N tokens and you're doing long appends past N, the runtime will miss secondary KV pages and re-fetch them synchronously. Increasing prefetch_window reduces synchronous misses at the cost of slightly higher memory.
[09:48] [09:48] Sofia: Also check if you have prefix aliasing — sometimes clients accidentally rewrite prefixes with small variations which defeat reuse heuristics.
[09:56] Priya: hmm we do some prompt templating that introduces trailing whitespace or timestamps; could be aliasing. We'll sanitize templates.
[10:03] Markus: For the repro harness you mentioned earlier — will Redwood run on our workload or we run locally?
[10:08] Daniel: Both. Ideally you run local repro to verify, then we run the same harness in a controlled infra so we can attach debuggers and test runtime flags quickly.
[10:18] [10:18] Speaker 2: random aside — thought about using LRU -> LFU hybrid?
[10:22] Daniel: We have adaptive eviction policies; LFU helps for prefixes with long-term reuse, LRU for recent items. For your pattern a LFU-LRU blend (multi-queue) is typically best. We'll propose configuration.
[10:34] Priya: Anything else about batching? We already use dynamic batching.
[10:38] Daniel: Dynamic batching is good; set per-route latency SLOs and a max_batch_age to limit queuing. Also consider 'latency-first' routing for heavy routes — route to nodes with lower KV load.
[10:50] Lydia: Is routing by KV-load available today?
[10:53] Daniel: We have an experimental routing key: route_by_kv_pressure. For Dedicated customers we can enable in beta.
[11:00] Priya: That could be helpful.
[11:03] [11:03] Sofia: We'll add enabling route_by_kv_pressure to the canary list.
[11:07] Markus: On instrumentation, you asked for kv.prefetch_hits — where do we surface that?
[11:11] Daniel: In the Redwood Console under model -> runtime -> kv metrics. We'll give you dashboard links and pre-built alerts.
[11:20] Priya: Great.
[11:22] [11:22] Quick interruption — network glitch for 20s, resumed.
[11:45] Daniel: To summarize proposed triage: 1) Short-term: reduce max_batch_size for heavy routes, increase kv.ttl for known hot prefixes, increase kv.prefix_shard_count, enable prefetch_window bump, enable soft-evict. 2) Mid-term: run A/B on compact-kv and mixed-KV precision, evaluate dedicated memory bump or NVMe local cache. 3) Long-term: consider Private on-prem for full isolation or we provide a specialized Dedicated SKU with higher kv memory.
[12:15] Priya: Sounds like a plan. For the short-term flags, any risk to turning them on?
[12:20] Daniel: Minimal risk; shard_count roll requires rolling restart but we do canary. soft-evict increases memory usage slightly. We'll provide exact expected overheads.
[12:32] Lydia: Very helpful. Can you also point to docs for safe rolling updates and for the kv config knobs?
[12:36] Sofia: Yes, I'll send the links — we'll include runtime flags, canary steps, and a checklist for metrics to watch.
[12:44] [12:44] Action item recap (auto):
- Daniel: run repro and collect detailed profiles
- Sofia: send pricing, runtime cookbook, and dashboard links
- Priya: upload anonymized prompts and traces

[12:58] Markus: One last thought — about prefix namespace separation. We'll want an API pattern to enforce tenant prefixing automatically. Is that supported?
[13:06] Daniel: You can use per-route namespace enforcement via the request header 'X-Redwood-Prefix-Namespace' or we can inject prefixes at the proxy layer. We'll send examples in the cookbook.
[13:20] Priya: Great, thanks.
[13:22] Sofia: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the canary plan and schedule a check-in after the initial triage next week.
[13:30] Lydia: Thanks all.
